prayer.text: O Sacrament most holy, O Sacrament divine, all praise and all thanksgiving be every moment thine.

cues.text: A Young Woman's Desperation

According to the tradition preserved in Alatri, a young woman troubled by a fading romance sought out a woman locally reputed for sorcery, hoping for some remedy that might restore her sweetheart's affection.
The remedy she was given, tradition holds, called for a consecrated host, to be used as an ingredient in a love potion.
A Host Concealed
At Mass, the account relates, the young woman received Holy Communion but did not consume the host, instead holding it in her mouth until she could conceal it in a cloth and carry it home.
There, tradition says, she kept it hidden for three days awaiting further instruction.
Flesh Where Bread Had Been
When she finally returned to the cloth, the young woman found not the host she had concealed but a piece of visibly bleeding human flesh.
Overcome, tradition holds, she confessed everything to the local bishop, Giovanni V of Alatri, surrendering the transformed relic to him.
A Papal Bull, Weeks Later
What sets Alatri apart from most medieval Eucharistic traditions is the survival of an actual papal document responding to the event almost immediately.
On March 13, 1228, Pope Gregory IX wrote to Bishop Giovanni in a bull known as Fraternitas tuae .
He addressed him as "venerable brother."
The pope noted that after three days, the young woman found the Body she had received in bread transformed into flesh, "as everyone has been able to verify with their own eyes," .
He instructed the bishop to treat both women with mercy, judging that they had acted more from weakness than malice.
Few Eucharistic accounts from this period rest on so direct and datable a piece of documentary evidence.
Legacy

We recognize in Gregory IX's own response something worth noting alongside the wonder itself: a pope inclined not toward condemnation but toward mercy, treating the young woman's desperate act as a failure of judgment rather than of faith.
The relic he wrote of remains today in Alatri's Cathedral of St. Paul the Apostle, displayed in a monstrance nearly eight centuries later.
Alatri's tradition reminds us that sacrilege was born of very human desperation—heartbreak, in this case—rather than hatred.

In the Church's own oldest surviving account, it was met with compassion rather than only judgment, alongside a sign the pope himself read as strengthening faith rather than merely punishing its absence.
